title: Maternal use of methamphetamine induces sex-dependent changes in myocardial gene expression in adult offspring.
ehr_evidence: The manuscript contains no data or description of human patients. All procedures involving animals were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Marshall University. (Data source was rat heart tissue: 'Hearts were then flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.')
summary: In an experimental animal study, pregnant Sprague-Dawley rats were injected with methamphetamine during gestation and RNA sequencing/Western blotting of adult offspring hearts revealed sex-dependent, persistent changes in myocardial gene expression.
key_findings: RNA sequencing identified 346 differentially expressed (FDR <0.01) mRNAs in adult hearts from prenatal methamphetamine exposure, with 74 changes common to both sexes, 184 occurring only in females, and 89 occurring only in males.
BDH1 protein expression was significantly decreased in hearts from both male (p < 0.01) and female (p < 0.05) offspring prenatally exposed to methamphetamine.
DDAH2 protein expression was significantly decreased in female hearts (p < 0.01) but was not significantly altered in adult male hearts.
Adult female offspring exhibited a greater number of methamphetamine-induced gene expression changes than males (184 vs 89).
captured_features: RNA sequencing (DESeq2, FDR <0.01, Log2 fold change)
Log2 fold change values and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values for differentially expressed genes
Western blot band intensities of DDAH2 and BDH1 normalized to GAPDH
population: Adult Sprague-Dawley rat offspring (males and females) prenatally exposed to methamphetamine in utero
limitations: Animal model (rats) limits direct human extrapolation
No overt contractile dysfunction or hypertrophy observed, so clinical significance of gene expression changes is unclear
